item.title: Switzerland-China: agreement to eliminate customs duties
item.description: Agreement for customs exemption on 99.8% of Swiss exports to China: estimated annual savings of CHF 244 million for Swiss companies.
item.content:encoded:
## In a nutshell - Updated trade agreement between Switzerland and China. - Elimination of tariffs on 99.8% of Swiss exports. - Estimated savings for exporters of CHF 244 million per year. - Inclusion of clauses on labour rights and the environment.
## Key facts - **What**: Revision of the bilateral free trade agreement. - When: Announced on Thursday, effective pending signature and approval. - Where: Bern, Switzerland. - Who: Federal Councillor Guy Parmelin and Minister Wang Wentao. - Amount: Savings of CHF 244 million per year. - Percentage: 99.8% of Swiss exports duty-free. - Percentage: 53.8% of exports currently duty-free.
Federal Councillor Guy Parmelin and Chinese Minister Wang Wentao announced the conclusion of negotiations for an enhanced trade agreement between Switzerland and China. The agreement, formalized through the signing of a memorandum of understanding in Bern, aims to eliminate tariff barriers that still weigh on bilateral trade. According to the federal authorities, the objective is to achieve exemption from customs duties for 99.8% of current Swiss exports to the Chinese market. This milestone represents a significant evolution compared to the current situation, where only 53.8% of Swiss goods benefit from this exemption. Bern estimates that, when fully operational, Swiss exporting companies will be able to achieve estimated total annual savings The analysis of the contents of the new agreement reveals an innovative approach that goes beyond the simple reduction of duties, introducing relevant social and environmental standards. Switzerland, through the work of the SECO (State Secretariat for Economic Affairs), insisted on the inclusion of binding provisions concerning compliance with the conventions of the International Labour Organization (ILO). This is a turning point in trade relations with Beijing, as it is the first time that China has accepted explicit clauses on the protection of workers' fundamental rights within a free trade agreement. At the same time, the chapter dedicated to environmental protection has been defined as one of the most ambitious ever negotiated by both parties. The commitments signed cover strategic sectors such as the transition to cleaner energies and the implementation of models related to the circular economy.
### Implications for the national economic system For Swiss companies, overcoming customs barriers represents a direct competitive advantage, in particular for sectors that have so far suffered partial or total limitations. The watchmaking and pharmaceutical sectors, pillars of the national economy, will benefit from more fluid and less onerous access. It is important to emphasize that the ratification procedure remains an essential step: the agreement must in fact be submitted to Parliament for approval.
## Useful tools to protect your net income To reduce FX leakage, compare [CHF-EUR exchange options](nav:exchange) and [banks for cross-border workers](nav:banks). The path to full implementation of the agreement still requires precise institutional steps before the new tariffs become applicable. Following the signing of the memorandum of understanding, the Federal Council must submit the final text to Parliament for official ratification. No specific dates have been provided for the parliamentary votes, but the government has indicated that the agreement should be formally signed by the end of the current year. For economic operators and workers concerned about the impact of these measures, the procedure includes an analysis phase during which parliamentary committees will evaluate technical details and environmental and social safeguard clauses. Therefore, companies involved in exports to the Chinese market must periodically check official SECO announcements for updates on the entry into force of individual tariff exemption stages.
### Steps and tools for updates For those operating in the trade sector or wishing to understand the impact of these changes on the labor market and business planning, the Federal Administration's website remains the primary source for customs procedures. Managing one's professional position, especially in a context of changing import and export policies affecting key sectors of the Swiss economy, requires constant attention to macroeconomic indicators. Although the agreement primarily concerns the trade of goods, the positive repercussions on the stability of the involved production sectors can also indirectly influence employment prospects. For those intending to evaluate their situation in relation to national market trends and wage dynamics, it is useful to consult reference tools. Access to up-to-date information on wage dynamics and economic trends can help better plan one's professional future. For an in-depth analysis of your remuneration in relation to the current economic context, you can use the [salary calculator](nav:calculator) to verify your position in the Swiss labor market.

item.title: Residence Permit B Bern: Requirements and Renewal
item.description: The B permit is renewable every year. Complete guide to requirements, necessary documents and renewal procedure at cantonal migration offices.

## In a nutshell - Permit B is a renewable residence document for residence in Switzerland - Managed by cantonal offices coordinated by the federal SEM - Renewable periodically with presentation of updated documentation - Distinguished from permit L (short duration, up to 1 year) and C (domicile)
## Key facts - **What**: Renewable residence permit in the Swiss SEM system - Category: Permit B of the Secretariat of State for Migration - Competent body: Cantonal Office of Migration of each canton - Validity: Renewable, non-perpetual; periodic duration - Rights: Legal residence, work in Switzerland, access to public services
The B residence permit is the administrative instrument that allows a foreigner to legally reside in Switzerland for reasons of work, family reunification or other stable purposes — unlike the L permit, which authorizes short stays of up to one year. In the Swiss migration system managed by the State Secretariat for Migration (SEM), the B permit represents an intermediate category between the L permit (short duration) and the C permit (domicile), the latter reserved for those who have accumulated a certain number of years of stable residence.
The main feature of the B permit is its renewability: it is not a permanent document, but periodically (usually every year) requires verification and renewal at the competent cantonal migration office. This renewability means that those who ### Practical implications of the B permit in Switzerland
Having a B permit in Switzerland entails specific rights and duties that affect the daily, tax and social security life of those who reside in the country. Unlike the L permit, designed for short and precarious stays, the B permit legitimizes a stable residence and gives access to many civil and social rights, although not to federal political rights (voting, elections).
On the **employment** front, a B permit holder can work in Switzerland for Swiss employers, with protection from Swiss labour law. This means access to guarantees: maximum hours 45 hours per week in industry/offices/sales, or 50 hours in other sectors; minimum 4 weeks of annual leave (5 for those under 20). The salary contributions — AVS/AI/IPG (5.3% employee, 10.6% total with employer), AD/AC (1.1% up to the annual ceiling), LAINF/LAA accident insurance (0.7-1.5% depending on the sector), and the third social security pillar LPP/BVG — follow the same rules applied to Swiss citizens.
On the tax front, a B permit holder is subject to Swiss taxation on three levels: direct federal tax (DFI), cantonal tax and municipal tax. In the canton of Bern, as in every canton, there are specific cantonal rates and municipal multipliers: each municipality applies a multiplier to the cantonal rate. ## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). ### How to request a B Permit
The request for a B Permit occurs at the cantonal level. Here are the general steps that are followed in most cantons, including Bern:
**Step 1: Gather supporting documents**
Before visiting the cantonal migration office, it is necessary to prepare the supporting documents. Generally, the following are required: a valid passport or recognized identity document, a signed employment contract from the Swiss employer (or a job offer letter), a declaration of residence or rental agreement that proves a stable residence, a certificate of no pending criminal record from the country of origin (if required), and cantonal request forms completed.
Step 2: Submit the application to the cantonal office
In the canton of Bern, the competent office is the cantonal migration office. The application must be submitted in accordance with the specific modalities specified by the canton. It is essential to respect the deadlines and attach all the required documentation, otherwise the application will be postponed until completion.
Step 3: Examination and decision phase
The office examines the documentation, verifies that the employment contract is in order, and checks for any exclusion grounds. The examination time varies from a few days to 4-6 weeks, depending on the workload of the cantonal office.
Step 4: Permit collection or notification of denial
If approved, the holder will receive the B Permit. If denied, they will receive a notification with the reasons for the denial and the possibility of appealing within specific terms.
### Renewal of the B Permit
The B Permit must be renewed periodically. The validity period depends on the individual situation and cantonal laws, but renewal is usually required annually. Before the expiration date (usually 30-60 days), the holder must submit a new renewal application with updated documentation: current employment contract, updated residence declaration, and a good conduct certificate if required by the canton.
The renewal process follows a similar procedure to the initial request and is usually faster, as the file is already known to the office.
### Rights and duties during the validity of the permit
During the validity of the B Permit, the holder has the duty to maintain compliance with: tax obligations (submitting an annual tax return in the canton of residence), notification obligations (notifying changes in address or employer to the migration office), health insurance (maintaining an active LAMal coverage), and pension contributions (regularly paying AVS/AI and LPP contributions through the employer).
In the event of non-renewal, the permit expires, and residence becomes illegal. Therefore, it is recommended to monitor deadlines and initiate the renewal procedure in advance.
### Useful tools for B Permit holders
To calculate the net salary of your salary in Switzerland, considering AVS, LPP, and cantonal/municipal taxes, consult the [salary calculator](nav:calculator). This tool allows you to estimate how much will remain in your paycheck after all social and fiscal deductions, useful for planning your budget once established in Bern with a B Permit. If you have doubts about procedure, documentation, or specific deadlines of the canton of Bern, the cantonal migration office is the authorized source. Each canton has slightly different rules, and the office staff can provide exact instructions for your situation.

item.description: Compensation fund, AVH annuity and supplementary benefits in the Canton of Zurich. Complete guide to the first pillar: calculation, contribution gaps, vital minimum.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - The Zurich cantonal compensation fund manages the AVS contributions of workers and employers - The first pillar covers employees and self-employed with fixed federal rates - Complementary benefits fill the contribution gaps to ensure a minimum vital
## Key facts - **What**: Mandatory social security system in the Canton of Zurich - Where: Zurich cantonal compensation fund (CVZ) - Who: All residents and employed and self-employed workers in Zurich - AVS rate: 5.3% for the employee, 10.6% total (employer + employee) - Function: Calculation of the pension and coverage of gaps through complementary benefits
### The first pillar in the Canton of Zurich
In the Canton of Zurich, the cantonal compensation fund manages the first pillar (AVS/AI) for resident population and employed and self-employed workers. The fund acts as an intermediary between the payers and the state, ensuring that contributions are recorded correctly and that pensions are calculated based on the contribution history of each insured person.
The first pillar is a mandatory system: anyone working in Switzerland automatically pays contributions from their salary. For employees, the rate is 5.3% on gross salary, while the employer pays an additional 5.3%, for a total of 10.6%. Self-employed individuals pay 9.8% based on income. These contributions finance both old-age insurance (AVS) and disability insurance (AI) and the unemployment benefit fund.
The Zurich cantonal compensation fund is responsible for registering contributions, communicating data to the Federal Office of Social Insurance (UFAS/BSV), and managing the local contribution flow administration. This ensures that each working year is correctly documented in the individual account of the insured person. Accessing [first pillar opportunities](nav:pension) allows understanding how each paid contribution is transformed into pension entitlement.
### How the AVS pension is calculated
The AVS pension in the Canton of Zurich is based on three key elements: the average salary realized during the career (calculated by averaging over all years of contribution), the number of effective years of contribution, and the conversion rate applied to the pensionable age (from 63 to 70 years, depending on the choice of the insured person).
A contribution gap occurs when a year is not entirely covered by AVS payments. Gaps can result from periods of unemployment, illness, study, absence from work, or career interruptions for personal or family reasons. Even if a gap is recorded, it can be partially covered by subsequent voluntary payments or recognized family income.
The complementary benefit (PC) was designed specifically to fill these gaps: it guarantees a minimum vital income to those with an insufficient AVS pension and limited resources. In the Canton of Zurich, PC are granted according to federal criteria (Federal Law on Complementary Benefits) and managed jointly by canton and municipalities. ### What are contribution gaps and how are they identified
A contribution gap is a year in which a person has paid less than the AVS contribution ceiling, or has not paid at all. As a hypothetical example, if a person has stopped work for an entire year without payouts, thatyear will be recorded as a total gap in the individual account. If, on the other hand, you have worked for only six months, the gap will be partial.
The individual account is the central document of each insured: it contains the record of all contributions paid year by year, from the first day of work until retirement. Each person has the right to check their individual account with the cantonal clearing house in Zurich, on a regular basis (typically every 5-10 years, or upon informal request).
In the Canton of Zurich, it is possible to consult the individual account directly with the CVZ (Cassa di Compensazione Zurichese) in person, or through the online portal made available by the Cassa and the federal system. It is important to check your account at least a few years before retirement, to identify any gaps and have time to correct them or plan a voluntary payment strategy. If you discover an error or missing contribution, you can report it directly to the CVZ and initiate an administrative correction.

item.title: AVS Income in Zurich: how the first pillar works
item.description: Guide to the AVS system in the Canton of Zurich: compensation fund, pension calculation, contribution gaps and supplementary benefits for the minimum living wage.

## In a nutshell
- The AVS is the first pillar of Swiss social security - Managed by cantonal clearing houses (one per canton) - Supplementary benefits supplement the annuity for the minimum living
## Key facts
- **What**: AVS (first pillar), complementary services (PC/EL) - Where: Canton Zurich, via cantonal clearing house - Who: UFAS/BSV federal; cantonal fund; insure - How: Contributions paid (5.3% employee + 5.3% employer), accreditation, recognition of gaps
In the Canton of Zurich, the old-age pension system is divided into two complementary levels: the AVS (first pillar) and the complementary benefits (PC), both managed by the cantonal compensation fund.
The AVS represents the basis of social protection: it is financed through compulsory contributions (5.3% borne by the employee, 5.3% by the employer, on wages up to the federally fixed annual ceiling) and covers the risks of old age, disability and death of the family. The cantonal compensation fund of Zurich is the institution that centralizes payments, credits contribution periods, and pays annuities to those who have reached the reference age.
However, the AVS annuity is not always sufficient to cover the vital minimum. This includes supplementary benefits, financed by general taxes (not contributions), which supplement the AVS income if the insured's income and assets remain below the coverage threshold.
One ## Complementary services: how they cover the vital minimum
Complementary benefits (PC) are the mechanism that ensures economic dignity to those who are entitled to an AVS annuity but do not reach the living minimum. In Zurich, as in all Swiss cantons, the living minimum is defined by federal tariffs, but the cantonal administration coordinates with the compensation fund for the disbursement.
To access PCs, the amount of the AVS annuity (plus any other sources of income or equity) must remain below the coverage threshold. The "minimum living" includes: accommodation, food, clothing, medical care, essential expenses.
Unlike the AVS, which is contributory right, PCs are welfare benefits: the funding comes from taxes (50% Confederation, 50% canton), not from contributions. This means that even those who have paid few contributions, or who have long periods of gaps, can access PCs if income is insufficient.
### Scenario: AVS income reduced by contribution gaps
An insured who has reached the reference age may find an AVS annuity lower than expected for several reasons: - Non-insurance periods (e.g. unaffiliated self-employment) - Breaks due to prolonged unemployment without recognised contributions - Years of contribution less than 44 years (total from 1948 to 2024 for those who turn 65 in 2024)
In these cases, the Zurich Compensation Fund examines whether gaps can
## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). ## Procedure: How to Request AVS Pension and PCs in Zurich
### Step 1: Gathering Contributory Documents
About 3-4 months before the reference age (65 for men, 64 for women, subject to ongoing changes), request the professional career certificate from the Zurich Compensation Fund. You can do this: - Online, through the myAVS/miAVS portal (with Swiss digital certificate) - By mail, downloading the form from the Zurich fund's website - In person at the fund's office
The fund will inform you of: - Accredited years - Identified gaps (and if they can be recognized) - Estimated pension amount
### Step 2: Filling Gaps if Possible
If you identify gaps, consider: - **Voluntary LPP redemption**: If you were a freelance professional, you can redeem missing periods in the second pillar within a year of requesting the pension - Bonuses for unpaid work: If you cared for family members (young children, elderly parents), you can request accreditation of periods - Periods abroad: If you worked abroad with a Swiss spouse, some periods may be recognized
Contact the Zurich fund directly: they have experts who examine each case individually
### Step 3: AVS Pension Request
About a month before the reference age, submit the pension request (form available on the fund's website). The request must be submitted by mail or online. Attach: - Career certificate (obtained in step 1) - Copy of identification document - Declaration of current income (if still working)
### Step 4: If the pension does not cover the minimum vital amount → PC Request
Receive the decision on the pension. If the amount is low (often due to unfillable gaps), contact the Zurich Canton's Complementary Benefits Service (sometimes hosted at the fund's office itself).
Documents for the PC request: - Letter of AVS pension grant - Patrimonial declaration (immovable property, savings, securities) - Documentation of housing expenses (rental contract / property certificate) - Documentation of uncovered medical expenses
### Deadlines and Contacts
The decision on the AVS pension usually arrives within 30-60 days of the request. PCs must be requested once the AVS pension is definitively known.
Use the [AVS Calculator](nav:pension) to estimate your pension based on contributions paid in Switzerland. Enter your professional career data and the system will show a projection of the expected pension, helping you evaluate whether filling gaps is beneficial.
Also, consult the [Guide to the Cost of Living in Switzerland](nav:cost-of-living) to understand how the minimum vital amount varies by canton and what support measures are available in your situation.

item.description: Residence permit B Canton Bern: requirements, documentation, duration and renewal procedure. Complete and step-by-step guidance from SEM authority.

## In a nutshell - Permit B: renewable residence for foreigners in Switzerland with intermediate duration - Variable duration: renovation depends on work and residential continuity - Non-automatic renewal: submit application 3-6 months before expiry - Cantonal migration office Bern: competent authority for permit management
## Key facts - **What**: Residence permit B (renewable) for foreigners - Where: Canton Bern, cantonal migration authority management - Who: SEM (State Secretariat for Migration) coordinates, cantons administer - Nature: Intermediate and renewable residence, other than L (short) and C (permanent residence) - Requirements: Stable professional employment and suitable accommodation in the canton - Renewal: Non-automatic, case-by-case assessment
Residence permit B is one of the three main pillars of the Swiss migration system for foreigners. Unlike the L permit (short duration up to 1 year, non-renewable) and the C permit (stable domicile for 10 years of residence, or 5 years for EU/EFTA citizens), the B permit allows a residence of an intermediate duration entirely renewable based on the work and residential situation of the holder.
In the Canton of Bern, as in all Swiss cantons, the administrative management of residence permits is the responsibility of the cantonal migration office, in coordination with the State Secretariat for Migration (SEM) at the federal level. This means that any question of ### Requirements and documentation for permit B
The application for a B residence permit — both initial and renewal — is based on well-defined requirements at national level, although their concrete application may vary slightly between cantons. The foreigner must first demonstrate that he has a stable professional employment, usually proven by an employment contract or documentation from the employer. Secondly, you must prove the availability of suitable accommodation in the Canton of Bern, which complies with the cantonal regulations on housing quality.
The Bernese cantonal migration office typically requires the following documentation for a renewal application:
- Employment contract valid and confirmed by the employer - Proof of accommodation (duly registered lease, landlord's certificate, or equivalent) - Valid passport and photocopy - Criminal certificates from the federal authorities and the authority of the country of origin (if applicable) - Income tax return for the last 2 years or bank certificate attesting livelihood capacity - Cantonal application form completed and signed
If during the period of leave the holder has changed employer or accommodation, he must promptly notify and attach the new documentation. Major changes (job loss, change of accommodation in another municipality) may affect the outcome of the renewal.

## Recommended tools For an updated estimate, use the [net salary calculator](nav:calculator) and the [CHF-EUR exchange comparator](nav:exchange). ### Procedure step-by-step for renewal
Step 1: Advance verification (4-6 months before expiration) Contact the Bernese cantonal migration office (contact information is usually available on the canton's website in the migration section). Verify the required documentation for your specific case, as individual situations (change of employer, change of residence, etc.) may have slightly different requirements.
Step 2: Collection and preparation of documentation Prepare an updated employment contract (recent, signed), rental contract (or property certificate if owner), original passport and copy, penal certificates from the competent authorities, tax declaration for the last 2 years. If you changed employers during the current permit, ensure that the new contract is registered with the cantonal authorities and that the previous employer has formally notified the end of the employment relationship.
Step 3: Submission of the renewal application Submit the application to the Bernese cantonal migration office following the indicated procedures (paper-based, electronic, or mixed). Attach all required documentation in duplicate. It is recommended to obtain a receipt of receipt of the application, even if not mandatory.
**Step 4: Administrative examination The office will examine the application and documents. If the documentation is incomplete, it will contact the applicant for integration (usually 2-3 weeks to complete). If everything is in order, the examination will proceed to completion.
Step 5: Notification of outcome The office will communicate the outcome (approval, rejection, or approval with conditions) usually by official letter. If approved, you will receive a new permit document with a new expiration date (validity usually 1-5 years, at the discretion of the office based on the stability of the employment situation).
### Critical deadlines
The renewal application must be submitted before the formal expiration of the B permit. If you forget to renew and the permit expires, the administrative situation becomes irregular: the right to residence and the right to work cease immediately. Therefore, mark a reminder in your calendar at least 5-6 months before the expiration date indicated on the permit.
If the permit expires during the examination of the renewal application, you are generally protected by the 'transitional rule' — authorized to continue residence and work until the examination is completed — but this protection is not always guaranteed. It is recommended to check directly with the cantonal office to confirm applicability in your specific case.
### Competent office and resources
The Bernese cantonal migration office is the sole competent authority for all matters related to residence permits (granting, renewal, modification, cancellation, appeals). You can contact them directly via the published phone number or email on the website of the Republic and Canton of Bern, in the administration section.

item.description: How the first AVS pillar works in the Canton of Zurich: compensation fund, annuity calculation, gaps and supplementary benefits for the living minimum.

## In a nutshell - The AVS is the first pillar of Swiss social security, administered locally by cantonal coffers - In the canton of Zurich, the compensation fund manages the contributions and the calculation of the annuity - Supplementary benefits cover the minimum life for those with insufficient income - Contribution gaps can be filled with voluntary payments
## Key facts - **What**: Administration of the first pillar of social security (AVS) at cantonal level - Who: Zurich Canton Compensation Fund (public body under UFAS/BSV supervision) - Where: Canton Zurich - When: Permanent system, updated annually for inflation - Amount: Contributions 5.3% employee, 10.6% total with employer
### L'AVS and the Zurich Compensation Fund
Old-age and survivors' insurance (AVS) is the first pillar of Swiss social security. It is not run by a single federal office, but by decentralised compensation funds at cantonal level: each canton, including Zurich, has its own fund that administers residents' contributions and calculates old-age and survivors' annuities.
The cantonal compensation fund is a public body under federal law that operates under the supervision of the Federal Office of Social Insurance (UFAS/BSV). In the Canton of Zurich, the local treasury collects contributions paid by employees (5.3% of gross salary) and employers (5.3% of gross salary), for a total of 10.6%. These payments are ### Contribution gaps and how to fill them
A contribution gap is a year in which no AVS contributions have been paid. They can occur for various reasons: unemployment, parental leave, prolonged illness without allowance, studies, or simply periods of inactivity not covered by social benefits. Each gap year reduces the final AVS annuity.
In the Canton of Zurich, as in the rest of Switzerland, it is possible to fill the contribution gaps by making voluntary contributions. The procedure is simple: you go to the cantonal compensation fund, which calculates the amount due for the missing years, applies default interest (if the payment is delayed), and communicates the total. The payment can be made in a single payment or in installments, according to agreements with the cashier.
The advantage of filling the gaps is obvious: each year added increases the future income. If a person has worked 40 years out of 44 possible career years (21-65 years), they have a 4-year gap. Paying voluntary contributions for those 4 years brings back the complete career, proportionally increasing the income.
The Canton of Zurich Compensation Fund provides online tools and consultants to calculate the cost of voluntary payment and simulate the impact on future income. It is advisable to make this calculation before choosing whether or not to pay, because the cost can be significant (it depends on the salary insured and the number of years).

The procedure to obtain the AVS pension begins a few months before the retirement age. In the Canton of Zurich, approximately 2-3 months before reaching the reference age (65 for men, 64 for women during this period), the compensation fund sends an official notification to the resident with an extract of their contribution history calculated up to that point. This document contains the estimated monthly pension based on the available data.
Those who receive the notification must verify it: check that all contribution years are recorded, that the insured salaries correspond to those declared, and that there are no unexplained gaps. There are no exceptions for Zurich, Geneva, Bern, or other cantons: tenancy law is federal.
### Security deposit: maximum 3 months The landlord may request a security deposit up to a limit of three months' rent. This limit is mandatory. The deposit must be placed in a blocked account in the tenant's name at a banking institution or the competent cantonal office. This protects the tenant from arbitrary withholding: the money remains theirs unless there are documented damages or proven arrears. A request for a deposit exceeding three months is illegitimate, and the tenant may refuse it.
### Termination: only with official form An oral, informal, or email termination is not valid. In the canton of Zurich, the landlord must notify the termination using the official cantonal form. This formal requirement protects both parties, ensuring notification certainty and compliance with legal deadlines. Termination notice periods are strict: one month for the first year of tenancy; two months from the second to the ninth year; three months starting from the tenth year. A termination without the official form does not start the notice period, and the tenant may contest it.
### Rent contestation within 30 days If the tenant contests the initial rent, they have thirty days to contact the conciliation authority for tenancy matters in the canton of Zurich. This is a public extrajudicial procedure, not a private one: the authority examines whether the rent is manifestly disproportionate to the situation. The deadline is peremptory: after thirty days, the right to contest expires. Understanding the [cost of living in Switzerland](nav:cost-of-living) and how rents affect your finances is the first step toward conscious living. ### What happens if the landlord does not respect federal limits
Many conflicts arise from non-compliance with federal regulations. If a landlord requests four or five months of security deposit, they are acting against the law: the tenant can contest this and request the return of the excess amount. If the landlord sends a termination notice without the official form, the notice period does not begin to count, protecting the tenant from legal surprises. This protection is structural and does not depend on the will of the individual landlord.

In the canton of Zurich, there is a public conciliation authority that mediates between the tenant and the landlord. It is not a court, but an administrative body that verifies contractual compliance with the law. If the rent seems unjustified compared to the apartment's characteristics (size, location, condition, services), the authority can reject the rent and propose a fair amount. The decisions of the conciliation authority are not binding in the event of an appeal to the court, but they serve as a starting point and often resolve the dispute. Turning to this authority is free and fast compared to judicial proceedings.
### Equal protection throughout Switzerland
A tenant living in Zurich, another in Lausanne, and a third in Lugano have identical protection rights under federal law. There are no exemptions or exceptions for rich or poor, rural or urban cantons. This national uniformity is a strength of the Swiss system: residential mobility does not entail substantial changes in fundamental rights. Certainly, the rental market is more competitive in Zurich and Geneva than in more peripheral cantons, but the rules on forms, terms, and limits remain the same.

### The conflict between the two bodies
A real arm wrestling with the remuneration of the heads of the sickness funds. The Health Commission of the National Council (CSSS-N) is clearly opposed to the Federal Council, which had proposed in recent days to guide the salaries of managers at the level of a federal councilor — about 480 thousand francs a year — to "simplify the system".
For CSSS-N that figure is too high. The project, the result of the parliamentary initiative of the socialist Bapstiste Hurni, senator of Neuchâtel, instead provides for anchoring the salary ceilings to the highest remunerations paid within the Federal Administration, taking into account the actual number of insured and the average costs per insured of the individual ## Implications for premium payers
When deciding on the maximum salary ceiling of the heads of the sickness funds, the impact is reflected — directly or indirectly — on the pockets of those who pay the premiums. An inflated remuneration of the managers represents a cost that is amortized on the basis of the policyholders. CSSS-N has understood this link well: limiting salaries to the levels of the Federal Administration (rather than the Federal Councillors) means containing the overall operating costs of the coffers. It is not just a matter of principle, but of economic rationality that directly affects the balance sheet of Swiss households.

The **CSSS-N proposes** to anchor the ceilings to the highest salaries of the Federal Administration, with adjustment according to the number of policyholders and the average costs of each fund. This creates a flexible but contained parameter, calibrated on the actual operational size of each fund.
The Federal Council claims to simply equate about CHF 480,000 a year to the salaries of a federal councillor. Easier administratively, but potentially more onerous for the system.

item.title: Appenzello Interno Scholarships: a guide to funding
item.description: In the Inner Appenzell Canton, scholarships and study loans are available for those who continue their training after compulsory schooling. Find out how to apply.
item.content:encoded:
## Brief Overview - In the Canton of Appenzell Innerrhoden, there are scholarships available for deserving and economically disadvantaged students - The Swiss system is managed autonomously by each canton with different criteria - Details on requirements and amounts should be requested directly from the competent cantonal office - Scholarships are a tool for equity in access to higher education
## Key Facts - **What**: Scholarships and study loans - Where: Canton of Appenzell Innerrhoden (Northeastern Switzerland) - Who: Cantonal administration - For whom: Students pursuing post-obligatory education - System: Autonomous management for each Swiss canton
In the Canton of Appenzell Innerrhoden, as in every other Swiss canton, there are public funding mechanisms for students who wish to continue their education after compulsory schooling. Unlike countries with centralized systems, Switzerland entrusts each canton with full responsibility for defining access criteria, maximum amounts, and candidate application procedures.
This administrative federalism means that the conditions for obtaining a scholarship in Appenzell Innerrhoden can differ significantly from those of other cantons. A student transferring from one canton to another may find themselves in very different economic situations: one canton offers generous scholarships to those with a moderate family income, while another provides aid only in cases of extreme difficulty.
Scholarships play an important role in ensuring equitable access to education: they allow students from families with limited living costs to pursue vocational training or higher education without burdening their family's economic capacity entirely.
### Common criteria in the Swiss system
Although we do not have access to the specific criteria of the Canton of Appenzell Innerrhoden in this article, it is useful to illustrate the common factors considered by most Swiss cantons.
Family income is the most important criterion: each canton defines an annual threshold below which students can apply. Academic merit is often a valuation factor: good grades can increase the scholarship amount or allow access to those with slightly above-threshold income. Citizenship is relevant: most cantons recognize the right of Swiss citizens and, with more restrictive conditions, EU/EFTA citizens and regularly resident foreigners.
The number of dependents and living situation can also affect the decision to grant aid. The underlying idea is that scholarships should reach those who truly need economic assistance, while those with sufficient family resources do not receive public funding. ### Differences between cantons and practical implications
The federal scholarship system generates significant differences between cantons. A critical aspect for those living in Switzerland is that the right to a scholarship does not depend solely on academic ability or economic need, but also on the canton of residence and the one in which one studies.
For those who have children who wish to pursue their studies, it is essential to inform themselves promptly about the conditions in the canton of residence. Not doing so means missing deadlines for submission and, as a result, opportunities for funding for an entire academic year.
In the Canton of Inner Appenzell, the competence in managing scholarships remains entirely within the cantonal administration. This implies that there is no appeal to a federal authority in the event of a denial of a scholarship: the appeal remains within the cantonal administrative procedure according to the rules defined locally.
### Scholarships versus study loans: differences in operation
A fundamental aspect is the difference between scholarships and study loans. Scholarships are non-repayable contributions: they do not need to be repaid. Loans, on the other hand, are money that the student receives with the obligation to repay it over time, often with reduced or even zero interest rates.
Many Swiss cantons offer both options: a student can receive a part of the funding as a scholarship (non-repayable) and a part as a loan (to be repaid). This combination seeks to balance equity (providing real help to those in need) with financial sustainability (avoiding the fact that future generations of taxpayers finance indefinitely young people who have already completed their studies).
### Effects on social mobility and access to education
The availability of public funding for studies directly affects the student's cost of living and their ability to focus on the academic path. A student who receives a scholarship or an easy loan has less economic pressure and can devote themselves completely to their studies, without the need to perform parallel work that could compromise their performance.
This also affects social mobility: it facilitates access to higher education for children of families with modest incomes, reducing the gap between those who can afford private studies and those who rely on public aid. In a context where education is one of the main levers of socio-economic mobility, the scholarship system represents a public investment in social cohesion.

## In a nutshell - gfs.bern survey: 3-16 August 2026, 17,212 people - Neutrality: 54% against, 42% in favour (73% decision-making) - Power supply: 49% against, 47% in favour, 4% undecided - Vote on September 27, 2026
## Key facts - **What**: Survey on two Swiss federal initiatives (neutrality, food) - When: 3-16 August 2026, vote 27 September 2026 - Where: Switzerland (national champion) - Who: Institute gfs.bern for SRH, 17,212 people - Amount: Neutrality 54% no / 42% yes; Power 49% no / 47% yes
The first SSR gfs.bern survey of federal votes on September 27 paints a clear picture for the neutrality initiative and uncertain for the food initiative. Conducted from 3 to 16 August on 17,212 people, the survey shows the rejection of the initiative promoted by the UDC with 54% against and 42% in favour, while for the food initiative a head-to-head emerges with 49% against, 47% in favour and 4% undecided. A margin of error of 2.8 percentage points underscores the uncertainty about power.
### Neutrality Initiative
On neutrality, 73% of respondents already have clear ideas — a sign of advanced opinion formation. Within the parties, the gaps are marked: among the supporters of the UDC (promoter of the initiative), 86% support yes. In the other parties, opposites clearly prevail, indicating a deep fracture in the Swiss political coalition. The margin of error of 2.8 percentage points on the food initiative highlights how close the vote is. With 49% against and 47% in favor, a shift of just 2-3 points would change the outcome. The fact that 40% of voters have not yet formed a clear opinion leaves room for campaigns, media, and communication in the months leading up to September 27. The initiative on neutrality, on the other hand, shows a polarized electorate: 73% have clear ideas, which reduces the space for significant changes in opinion. However, Switzerland's Italian-speaking region with its 55% in favor stands out from the national rejection (54%), reflecting different visions of Swiss sovereignty and the role of the Confederation in diplomacy and international relations. For the food initiative, the lines of political fracture are evident: Green Party voters (84%) and those of the Social Democratic Party (64%) converge, while members of FDP, UDC, and the Centre remain skeptical. The 18-39 age group and women, with a support of 54% and 55%, respectively, show that the theme of food autonomy and sustainability resonates with these demographic segments. The French-speaking region (57%) appears more sensitive to the issue than the national average (47%), while the Italian-speaking region (53%) remains moderately favorable but with lower consensus than the French-speaking region. ### How votes change in the last months The August surveys are a snapshot. In the 30 days leading up to September 27, the picture can evolve significantly. Media campaigns, public debates, and party communications will influence undecided voters on food — the 40% who have not yet formed a stable opinion — and may consolidate or weaken the 'no' on neutrality. The UDC, as promoter of the initiative on neutrality, will have an incentive to mobilize its members (86% in favor internally) and reach moderate undecided voters; on the other hand, supporters of a more flexible Switzerland in international politics will work to expand the current 54% of opponents. On food, the Greens and the Social Democrats will have to convince the Centre's moderate electorate — currently skeptical — that a 70% self-sufficiency target is realistic and manageable, not an isolated ideological ideal. ## In a nutshell - Permit L: authorization for up to 1 year for foreigners working temporarily in Switzerland - Federal management (SEM) with cantonal administrative competence - Possible extension according to work needs - Transition to permit B for longer residence stay
## Key facts - **What**: Short-term L permit for temporary admission of foreigners - Maximum duration: 1 year - Management: SEM (State Secretariat for Migration) with cantonal authorities - Canton: Inner Appenzell, cantonal operating procedure - Type: Temporary permit, renewable on request
### The L permit in the Swiss system for the admission of foreigners
The short-term L permit is a key tool of the Swiss temporary admission system for foreigners. Managed at the federal level by the State Secretariat for Migration (SEM), the L permit allows foreign nationals to stay and work in Switzerland for a maximum period of one year.
At the cantonal level, the Inner Appenzell Canton operates like the other Swiss cantons: it receives and processes L permit applications according to federal SEM legislation, coordinating with employers who intend to hire temporary foreign labour.
The L permit is distinguished from other Swiss permits by its purely temporary nature. Unlike the B permit (residence), which allows a renewable stay in the medium term, the L permit is designed for limited work needs ### Extension and transition to residence permit
A frequently asked question concerns whether the L permit can be extended. According to SEM regulations, the L permit does not extend automatically: each extension requires a new evaluation and formal request. The cantonal authorities of Appenzello Interno evaluate each request for an extension on the basis of the updated documentation provided by the employer and the foreigner.
The transition to more stable living situations is an important aspect. Those who hold an L permit and wish to settle longer in Switzerland can consider switching to the B permit (residence). The B permit is a renewable authorization that allows medium-long term stay, and is designed for those who intend to stay in Switzerland beyond the short period covered by the L permit.
The transition from permit L to permit B is not automatic, but requires a new application and evaluation by the authorities. Generally, the SEM evaluates the continuity of employment, the economic situation of the foreigner, and the support of the employer as relevant elements for the granting of the B permit. ## In a nutshell - Family allowances: monthly allowance for each dependent child in Switzerland - Appenzello Esterno applies the federal regime through a cantonal compensation fund - Application at the cashier affiliated to the employer or at the cantonal office
## Key facts - **What**: Family allowances (Familienzulagen) + training allowances for children in education - When: From the first day of the month of birth until the age of 25 (or end of training) - Where: Canton Appenzello Outer, north-eastern Switzerland - Who: Parents employed, self-employed, farmers with Swiss residence - Amount: Determined by federal law and cantonal decisions (variable by canton)
The Swiss system of family allowances is one of the pillars of national social security. These are monthly subsidies paid to parents who have dependent children, designed to cover part of the costs related to education, nutrition and development.
In the Canton of Appenzell Outermost, as in all Swiss cantons, family allowances are based on a federal regulatory framework, but find practical operation through cantonal compensation funds. This model makes it possible to maintain national cohesion while adapting the amounts and procedures to local realities.
### The federal-cantonal system of family allowances
Family allowances in Switzerland are not a discretionary benefit: they constitute a social right guaranteed by federal law to anyone who works ### Monthly amounts and cantonal variability
The amounts of family allowances are fixed by cantonal legislation and vary significantly from one canton to another. Outer Appenzel, like all Swiss cantons, autonomously determines the amounts applicable for: - **Child allowances **: paid monthly for each child up to a predetermined age (generally 16 years for children in general education) - Training allowances: amounts increased during periods of apprenticeship, vocational school or recognised universities, up to the age of 25
The exact amounts in force in the External Appenzell must be consulted directly at the competent compensation fund or on the canton portal, as these are adapted annually to correspond to the evolution of the cost of living and local political decisions.
### Duration and termination of the right
The right to family allowances starts from the first day of the month in which the child is born (or from the month in which the parent acquires residence in Switzerland, whichever is the later). The ordinary term corresponds to the child's 25th birthday.
However, if the child continues in a recognized training (apprenticeship, cantonal vocational school or university) beyond the age of 25, the training allowances continue until the end of the training itself. In the case of children with a disability recognised by the AI, the payment may be extended according to specific conditions.
###
## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). ### Procedure for Application: the Four Steps
The presentation of the family allowance application in Appenzello Esterno follows a standardized procedure, divided into four main phases.
Step 1: Identify the competent compensation fund
Most Swiss employers are affiliated with a compensation fund for a specific sector (industry, commerce and services, agriculture, domestic enterprises). If the employer is affiliated with one of these funds, the application must be submitted to that fund.
If the employer is not affiliated with any private compensation fund, the application must be submitted directly to the Appenzello Esterno cantonal compensation fund (Ausgleichskasse Appenzell Ausserrhoden). Contacts are available on the website www.ar.ch.
Step 2: Prepare the required documentation
To advance the application, the following documents must be gathered: - Birth certificate of the children (authentic copy) - Residence certificate in the Appenzello Esterno canton - Valid identification document of the applicant - Proof of occupational situation (employment contract for employees; AVS income statement for self-employed; extract from the commercial register for individual companies) - In the case of separated or divorced parents: court ruling attesting to the child's custody - In the case of unmarried paternity: registered declaration of paternity in the civil register
**Step 3: Submit the application
The application can be submitted through two channels: - Physical counter: at the competent compensation fund, during official opening hours - Online: many Swiss funds, including that of Appenzello Esterno, offer downloadable digital forms from the official website, with the possibility of telematic transmission
It is recommended to submit the application simultaneously with the child's birth or the start of the employment relationship, to avoid losing retroactive rights.
Step 4: Elaboration and first payment
Once the complete application with all documents has been received, the fund will process it within the prescribed terms (usually 30-60 days). The first allowance is paid in the month following the approval of the application, by bank transfer to the account indicated by the applicant.
### Continuity and variations over time
Once approved, the application remains active, and allowances are paid automatically every month until the right expires (25th birthday or end of training). It is not necessary to renew the application annually.
However, it is essential to notify the compensation fund promptly of any change in situation that may affect the right: - Birth of additional children - Change of employer or affiliated fund - Transfer of residence to another Swiss canton - End of training or change of school cycle - Separation, divorce, or modification of custody
Omitting these notifications may result in unjustified interruptions or errors in payments.
### Information and official contacts
For specific questions about family allowances in Appenzello Esterno, you can contact: - Company compensation fund: if the employer is affiliated with a private fund (consult the employment contract) - Appenzello Esterno cantonal compensation fund: www.ar.ch – Section "Family Allowances" or "Familienzulagen" - Civil registry office of the municipality of residence: for issues related to registration and anagraphic documents - Tax consultant or union: for clarification on tax aspects and coordination with other social benefits

## In a nutshell - Permit L allows work for up to 12 months, renewable if contract continues - Bound to specific employer, not transferable to other employers - Extension requests a new application from the cantonal office before the deadline - Switching to permit B depends on occupational continuity and employer willingness
## Key facts - **What**: L permit (short duration for foreign workers) - When: Valid 12 months from release, renewable - Where: Canton Appenzello Outer (eastern Switzerland) - Who: Cantonal Office for Migration + Federal SEM (State Secretariat for Migration) - Requirement: Employment contract with employer resident in Switzerland
The short-term L permit is the central regulatory instrument for the recruitment of foreign workers in the Swiss cantons. In the canton of Appenzello Esterno, economically oriented to the manufacturing and service sectors, the L permit allows employers to take on skills from abroad with defined administrative procedures and predetermined times.
The maximum duration of the L permit is 12 calendar months, according to the federal regulations of the State Secretariat for Migration (SEM). This means that the foreign worker obtains a residence title limited in time, strictly bound to the employment contract and the specific employer who sponsored the application.
### Federal and cantonal jurisdiction
In Outer Appenzell, as in all Swiss cantons, the management of permits follows a double ### Validity, renewal and extension
The L permit is valid for 12 months from the date of issue. This period ** is not automatically renewable**: the extension depends on the continuity of the employment relationship and the employer's willingness to maintain the hiring.
In Appenzello Esterno, renewal does not constitute a right acquired by the worker. Approximately 2-3 months before the expiry of the L permit, the employer must assess whether it intends to continue hiring. If yes, you must submit a new renewal application to the cantonal migration office, again providing the necessary documentation (updated contract, certificates of good life, attestations of qualifications).
The cantonal office re-examines the application according to the current federal and cantonal criteria: priority for the local labour market, absence of Swiss unemployed or citizens with a B permit for the same type of job, compliance with the sector's market wages. If the economic situation has changed (e.g. sector crisis, rising unemployment), renewal may be refused even if the employer intends to continue hiring.
### Transition to permit B (residence)
Once the L permit has expired, the foreign worker is not automatically entitled to a B (residence) permit. However, if the employment relationship continues and the employer wishes to maintain the hiring, it is possible to apply for a conversion from L permit to B permit.

## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). ### Procedure step-by-step to request the L permit
Step 1: Preliminary check at the canton
The employer contacts the Appenzello Esterno canton migration office to clarify the current requirements. Each canton has slightly different acceptance criteria based on the local labor market and occupational priorities. It is useful to check directly which sectors are currently open to the L permit and which documentation is required.
**Step 2: Collection of documentation**
The following documents are required (with variations by canton):
- Signed employment contract between the employer and foreign worker (must specify position, hours, salary, duration) - Certificate of good conduct/morality of the candidate foreigner (required by the country of origin or SEM) - Documentation attesting professional qualifications (diplomas, certificates, experience certificates) - Identification documents and valid passport - Proof of the employer's contribution capacity (if required by the canton)
The employer is responsible for collecting the documentation before submission.
Step 3: Submission of the application
The formal request is submitted to the Appenzello Esterno canton migration office. The office then transmits it to the federal SEM for final approval. It is recommended to keep a copy of the application and the receipt of submission.
Step 4: Instruction and approval
The instruction times are approximately 2-4 weeks for simple cases (e.g. seasonal employment clearly motivated, candidate from a country with facilitated agreements). More complex cases may require 6-8 weeks or more.
Step 5: Issuance of the L permit
Once approved, the application generates the formal L permit. The document is notified to the employer. The foreign worker can then enter or remain in Switzerland for the period of validity (12 months).
### Management of expiration and renewal
About 2-3 months before the L permit expiration, the employer should assess whether to renew. If they intend to maintain the employment:
- Contact the cantonal office again - Submit a new renewal application (with updated documentation) - Follow the same instruction procedure
If the employer does not renew, the worker has two options:
1. Leave the Swiss territory by the date of expiration of the permit 2. Find a new employer willing to sponsor a new L permit
The L permit does not allow the worker to remain in Switzerland without work after the expiration date.
### Where to contact in Appenzello Esterno
- Appenzello Esterno canton migration office: manages L permits at the cantonal level, evaluates conformity with local requirements, instructs first-level applications - Federal Migration Office (SEM): supervises general criteria, definitively approves permits on cantonal referral, manages federal matters of principle
For specific questions about the L permit and deadlines in Appenzello Esterno, the employer or their HR consultant should directly contact the cantonal office, which provides updated information on forms, administrative deadlines, and current seasonal criteria.
### Fiscal and social security implications
A frequently overlooked aspect is that a worker with an L permit, once employed in Switzerland, is subject to the same fiscal and social security obligations as any resident employee:
- AVS/AI/IPG: 5.3% at the expense of the employee, 10.6% total with employer contribution - Unemployment insurance (AD/AC): 1.1% up to annual maximum - LAMal/KVG (health insurance): mandatory within 3 months of arrival, premium per capita based on age and chosen franchise (300–2,500 CHF for adults) - Federal, cantonal, and communal taxes: according to income bracket and cantonal domicile
The employer is responsible for regular contributions and withholding taxes. To verify the fiscal impact of an L permit employment, you can consult the [salary calculator](nav:calculator) for an estimate of federal, cantonal, and communal taxation in Appenzello Esterno, or consult a tax consultant for specific details on the situation.

## In a nutshell - Permit C requires 10 years residence (5 for EU/EFTA) - Main criterion: cultural integration and employment stability - Application to the cantonal migration office with complete documentation - Early release in exceptional cases (marriage, startup, public service)
## Key facts - **What**: Residence permit C (permanent establishment) - Time requirement: 10 years (non-EU); 5 years (EU/EFTA) - Where: Canton of Outer Appenzell, Amt für Migration - Who: Resident foreigners, employees, self-employed, spouses of CH citizens - Integration: Employment stability, German language skills, criminal absence
Residence permit C is the most stable residence permit for those who decide to reside permanently in Switzerland. In the canton of Appenzello Esterno, as in the other cantons, the release follows uniform federal criteria defined by the Secretariat of State for Migration (SEM), although administrative procedures remain cantonal competence.
Unlike permit B (residence, renewable), permit C offers long-term legal stability as it is not subject to annual or biennial renewal. Those who reside permanently and meet the integration requirements can request a transfer from B to C at the cantonal migration office.
### Minimum Duration of Residence
The stay required varies depending on nationality: - Citizens of non-EU/EFTA States: normally 10 years of residence ### The administrative procedure in the canton of Appenzello Esterno
The application for a C permit must be submitted to the cantonal migration office (Departement Inneres, Amt für Migration). There is no federal procedure online: the application is paper or digital according to cantonal methods. The cantonal office instructs the file, acquires verification reports from the judicial police, the municipality of residence and the employer, then transmits the file to the SEM for opinion and formal approval.
### Full documentation required
The application typically includes: official cantonal form (available at the migration office or cantonal website), certificate of historical residence with certification of years of stay, copies of previous B permits, employment contract and pay slips or income certificate (last 2-3 years), certificate of the Swiss and foreign judicial police (no convictions), certificates of good conduct from abroad if applicable, letter of references from the employer, copy of passport or travel document, copy of current health insurance (LAMal).

**Phase 1: Document collection** (2-3 weeks) Gather all the documentation listed. Check the precise list on the Appenzello Esterno migration office website, as administrative changes may occur. Requesting certificates in advance (police record, employer, place of residence) involves waiting but no cost. The Swiss police record certificate is requested from the cantonal police office of residence; the foreign one from the competent authorities of the country of citizenship (the Swiss consulate can assist).
Phase 2: Filling out the form (1 week) The form must be filled out in German (official language of the canton). If you don't speak the language, you can request assistance from the migration office or a specialized consultant. A lawyer is not mandatory, but consulting can speed up the process and avoid formal errors.
Phase 3: Submitting the application (1 day) The application must be submitted in person at the Amt für Migration (offices in Herisau or Teufen according to the place of residence) or sent by certified mail with return receipt. Check the opening hours on the official website of the canton. Keep the delivery receipt and the file number.
Phase 4: Instructory phase (3-6 months) The office acquires information from the police, the municipality, the employer. The applicant may be summoned for an interview to verify integration criteria (interview conducted in German to verify language skills). It is advisable to maintain a stable address and contact during the investigation.
Phase 5: Notification of the decision The decision is notified in writing. In case of approval, the C permit is issued within a few working days (usually 5-10 days). In case of motivated rejection, it is possible to appeal to the cantonal administration within 30 days of notification.

All information is available free of charge at the cantonal migration office, the SEM website (www.sem.admin.ch) and the official portals of the cantons. It is not necessary to resort to paid intermediaries.

### The Swiss Academies Report
The Swiss Academies of Sciences have published a report estimating the costs of building a new nuclear power plant in Switzerland. The figure is surprisingly large: between 14 and 43 billion francs. How was it possible to reach such a wide range? The researchers examined two models of reactors of different sizes, calculating how costs could evolve under different conditions.
The starting costs used by the researchers are based on the current offers for large reactors, which are around 11,500 and 12,000 francs per kilowatt of power. From this basis, the scientists worked out two distinct scenarios.
In the optimistic scenario, the ratio ### Private sector financial capabilities
A crucial question naturally arises: could the Swiss private sector, represented by companies such as Axpo and BKW, directly finance such a venture? According to the report, the answer is very unlikely. The researchers believe that the construction of a new nuclear power plant in Switzerland will require considerable state support.
Specific financial risks are hardly sustainable by private actors alone. These include: extremely high initial investments (tens of billions), multi-year construction times without revenue, and uncertain electricity prices in the long amortization phase (which can last decades). In fact, international experiences show that in recent years it has only been possible to find private investors if the State has strongly mitigated the risks.
An additional element further complicates the Swiss framework: since potential managers such as Axpo and BKW are wholly or partially owned by the Cantons, in an investment of this caliber the public sector would still be indirectly involved and would help to bear the financial risks. In other words, even a 'private' solution would not really be: the cantonal public sector would remain a de facto co-investor.
### Implications for the Swiss economy
These astronomical costs have repercussions on federal and cantonal policy. An investment decision of this
## Useful tools to protect your net income To reduce FX leakage, compare [CHF-EUR exchange options](nav:exchange) and [banks for cross-border workers](nav:banks). ### Critical Decision Timeline
According to the report, the tender should be issued as early as the early 1930s if the goal is to provide electricity by the early 1950s. This means that the time window for a political decision is very narrow. A large nuclear power plant construction cycle typically takes 10-15 years, sometimes more with the delays seen in international projects. There are no wide margins for improvisation.
The fundamental assumption is a political decision of principle. Today this is still pending: the February 2026 referendum represents the first step of a democratic consultation on a strategic issue for Switzerland.
### Potential Contractors
In the event of an investment decision by the mid-2030s, the choice will presumably fall mainly on large third-generation water-cooled reactors (III/III+). Currently, only EDF/Framatome (France) and Westinghouse (United States) are in the running as contractors for Switzerland. Although they are currently building the most reactors worldwide, Chinese state groups (CNG, CNNC) and Russian (Rosatom) are excluded from Europe and Switzerland for geopolitical reasons. The South Korean KEPCO/KHNP, which certainly has experience, cannot currently offer its reactors in Europe independently due to a legal dispute with Westinghouse.
### And the Small Modular Reactors?
An alternative solution could come from the so-called 'mini-reactors' (Small Modular Reactors, SMR). However, the current answer is negative: there are no concrete empirical data on construction times and actual costs for SMR. Outside of China and Russia, this technology is mostly still in development or in the early stages of prototyping. A large project planned by the US producer NuScale was even abandoned before construction began due to a significant increase in cost predictions. For a political decision by Switzerland in the short term, SMR therefore do not offer a sufficiently solid economic data base.
### What to do now
Swiss citizens will have to express themselves in February 2026 on the referendum against the abolition of the ban on building new power plants. LAMal (Federal Health Insurance Act) is the mandatory health insurance in Switzerland. Each resident of the Canton of Outer Appenzell must stipulate it within three months of arrival in the canton. Unlike many European countries, the LAMal is not a state tax or a contribution automatically withheld from the paycheck: it is a private insurance paid directly by the insured to the sick fund of his choice.
Premiums are set by sickness funds based on federal criteria, but vary significantly from canton to canton and even from region to region within the same canton. In the Canton of Appenzell Outermost, as in all of Switzerland, each health insurance fund sets different rates depending on the age, gender and insurance model chosen.

Considering two scenarios: a single adult who chooses a CHF 300 deductible with a generalist basic model pays a higher monthly premium than those who choose a CHF 2,500 deductible. In the first case, if admitted for surgery, the fund covers 90% of the hospital bill after the first CHF 300 per year, limiting personal financial exposure. ## Key facts - **What**: Taxes on transfers of assets for inheritance and donation - Where: Cantonal tax administration of the canton of Schaffhausen - Who: Taxpayers who receive inheritances or donations - Competence: Cantonal law; there is no federal inheritance tax - Exemptions: Spouse and descendants have special tax status - Procedure: Declaration to the cantonal tax office within the established deadlines
In Switzerland, inheritance and gift taxes are not regulated by the Confederation: each canton has full jurisdiction and sets its own rates, deductions and exemptions. In the canton of Schaffhausen, as in all other cantons, the cantonal tax law governs how and when to pay inheritance tax and on any donations received. For those who inherit property or receive a donation, understanding the specific rules of their canton is essential to plan the asset transfer and comply with declaratory obligations.
The declaration of succession is the procedure by which the death of the testator is communicated to the cantonal tax authority and the assets from which the degree of taxation derives are declared. In the canton In the Swiss tax system, the taxation of successions and donations follows a fundamental principle: the degree of kinship between the deceased (or the donor) and the heir (or the donee). The closer the relationship, the lower the rate; the further away it is, the greater the tax burden.
In the canton of Schaffhausen, as in the other cantons:
- The **spouse** generally benefits from a total exemption or a very low rate. - Straight-line descendants (children, grandchildren of children) have low rates or partial exemptions. - Relatives in a straight ascending line (father, mother, grandparents) have an intermediate treatment. - Relatives in the collateral line (brothers, sisters, cousins) see medium or high rates. - Strangers (people not related by kinship) are taxed at the highest rates.
Each canton fixes multipliers and rates on a taxable basis calculated from the net worth of the heir or gift. item.title: AVS and complementary services Schaffhausen
item.description: The cantonal compensation fund manages the calculation of the AVS annuity and access to supplementary benefits in the Canton of Schaffhausen, guaranteeing the minimum living wage.
item.content:encoded:
## In a nutshell - The cantonal clearing house manages the AVS in Schaffhausen - Contribution gaps reduce income, filled by supplementary benefits - PC guarantees the minimum life for those with insufficient AVS income
## Key facts - **What**: AVS and complementary services in the Canton of Schaffhausen - When: From retirement age (65 years old men/women) - Where: Canton Schaffhausen (first pillar) - Who: Cantonal Compensation Fund, UFAS/BSV - Entitlement: At least three years of AVS contributions paid
Social security in the first pillar in Schaffhausen is based on two fundamental pillars: Old Age and Survivors Insurance (AVS) and the supplementary benefits system. The cantonal compensation fund of Schaffhausen manages the entire process of collection of contributions, [calcolo della rendita](nav:pension) and certification of pension rights for residents and policyholders in the territory. Every person who has paid at least three years of AVS contributions during their working career is entitled to an old-age pension upon reaching retirement age. The calculation of the annuity is based on the average of the annual incomes declared in the years of contribution. However, those who have paid contributions in a discontinuous manner — for long periods of unemployment, illness, care of family members or voluntary career interruption — accumulate contribution gaps that significantly reduce the monthly amount of the pension.
### Contribution gaps and calculation of annuity
Gaps ### How supplemental benefits cover the vital minimum
Complementary benefits are not a generic welfare measure, but an integrated system with the AVS itself. Once the monthly AVS annuity has been calculated, the office that investigates the PC application checks whether it covers the minimum subsistence requirement. The minimum is different from canton to canton, because it depends on local living conditions (rents, services, prices). In Schaffhausen, the minimum includes a fee for basic necessities (food, hygiene, transportation) and a housing allowance. If the AVS income is insufficient, the PC integrates the difference until it reaches the minimum. This logic also applies to people who receive not only the old-age pension, but also other benefits (AI disability pension, orphan's allowance). ## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). ### How to Request Additional Benefits in Schaffhausen, Switzerland
The procedure to obtain additional benefits in the Canton of Schaffhausen begins with the completion of an official form, available at the cantonal compensation office or through the online portal of the administration. The applicant must attach a series of documents:
- Copy of the AVS pension decision (sent annually by the AVS service) - Valid identity document - Certificate of residence in Schaffhausen (if recent transfer) - Detailed patrimonial declaration (accounts, investments, properties) - Documentation on housing expenses (rental contract or land register extract) - Any necessary medical certificate if special needs exist
The application must be submitted to the competent authority: the cantonal compensation office of Schaffhausen. The investigation process usually takes 2-3 months. During this time, the office may request clarifications or additional documents. If the application is accepted, the additional benefits will start from the first day of the month in which the office receives the complete application. The recognition is annual: the beneficiary must provide an updated income and patrimonial declaration every year to maintain the right. If the economic situation improves, the amount of additional benefits decreases proportionally; if it worsens, it may increase.
### Strategies for Closing Gaps and Planning Retirement
Those who know they have significant contributory gaps before reaching retirement age have the opportunity to pay voluntary contributions through the cantonal compensation office. This is particularly convenient in the years immediately preceding retirement, as each year of contributions paid increases the future pension. A search for contributions paid so far can be requested from the office: it provides an extract that lists all covered and uncovered periods. Based on this extract, it is possible to plan whether it is convenient to pay voluntary contributions to close the gaps rather than relying entirely on additional benefits. This evaluation is crucial: regularly requesting information on one's contributory position before retirement allows for informed decisions.
